description: Building a health monitoring software prototype for astronauts. I'm a software engineering graduate and medical student, passionate about code, health, and space. Looking for teammates skilled or interested in AI/ML, data analysis, UI/UX, web dev, or space exploration. Strong curiosity and teamwork required. Goal: Collaborate and build a practical, well-researched prototype together.
summary:
Vivonaut is an offline health companion that helps an astronaut notice, understand and act on changes in their own health when contact with Earth is delayed or lost. It turns NASA's hazards of long missions (radiation, isolation, distance, altered gravity and closed environments) into one loop: collect a reading, check how it was measured, compare it with the astronaut's own baseline, explain the result, guide the next step and follow up.
The app combines a Mission Day Briefing, a clickable body map, trend charts, a Monitoring Status board (Stable, Watch, Needs assessment, Alert, No data) and Viva, a companion who explains why every alert appeared, which rule fired and which source supports it. It prepares a Health Handover on the device, ready and queued for the next contact, and shows how a ground team would review it in a clearly labelled simulation. Nothing is hidden: rules without a published source are labelled DEMO, simulated data is labelled Simulated, and missing data is never shown as normal. Private wellbeing answers stay private unless shared.
Everything runs in one HTML file, with no internet, server or paid service. Vivonaut is an educational prototype, not a medical device, and is not made or endorsed by NASA.
details:
Vivonaut – Your Intelligent Health Companion in Space

Live demo: https://nhk25nhk-dotcom.github.io/Vivonaut/

Code, documentation and the complete list of sources: https://github.com/nhk25nhk-dotcom/Vivonaut

THE PROBLEM

On long missions, astronauts face NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity and hostile closed environments. When contact with the ground is delayed or lost, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting health changes in themselves. They need a tool that helps them notice a change, understand it and decide what to do next, without waiting for Earth.

WHAT VIVONAUT DOES

Vivonaut follows one workflow: Collect, Validate, Analyze, Assess, Guide, Track.

- Collect: heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, body temperature, body mass, sleep, mood, exercise and symptoms, plus eight optional checks (headache, food and fluid intake, motion sickness, dizziness on standing, vision, a reaction check, feeling connected and optional glucose). Radiation is a clearly labelled simulated dose. Every measurement has a short help card, because astronauts should not be assumed to know every method.

- Validate: an impossible value is never stored without a confirmation. Before a reading is interpreted, Viva checks how it was measured (recent exercise, posture, technique). A doubtful reading is marked "Needs verification", cannot change a status, and is repeated after a rest.

- Analyze: each indicator is compared with the astronaut's own baseline (the median of the first five calm readings, then frozen and changed only by a logged action) and with published reference ranges.

- Assess: a rule-based engine gives Stable, Watch, Needs assessment, Alert or No data. There is no health score, and missing data is never treated as normal.

- Guide: every alert says why it appeared ("How Viva decided": the rule, the values, the reference and its source), what to do next and who to contact. The guidance adapts to the link with Earth (Live, Delayed or Blackout) and to the mission environment (space station, spacecraft in transit, lunar base, Mars base).

- Track: every Watch or higher opens a follow-up. The app schedules a reassessment, compares before and after, and states honestly that a change cannot show what caused it.

THE EXPERIENCE

The app opens on a dashboard. A Mission Day Briefing gathers what is due today, what changed, the follow-ups waiting and the handover status. A clickable body map (brain, eyes, lungs, heart, immune, bones and muscles) shows only the status of its linked indicators, never a diagnosis. Viva, the companion, answers from prepared text and from the readings stored on the device: Ask Viva uses keyword and rule matching, with no language model, and can show why she answered as she did. Her voice uses the browser's built-in text-to-speech, is off by default, and captions are always on. Mission tasks, a weekly streak, goals and a timeline keep the routine engaging.

The Health Handover is built from the app's own data (readings, alerts, changes, missing information), stored on the device when contact is lost, and marked "ready and queued, not sent". A Ground view shows how a ground team would review it, with a simulated delay. It is a simulation: nothing is transmitted. An Emergency Center is a fixed, clearly labelled educational simulation, never a medical protocol. A Blood results screen is a simulated demonstration with fictional data, to show the concept of point-of-care analysis. Vivonaut analyses no blood and connects to no device. A Guided Demo plays three prepared scenarios in about two minutes, with captions, on a scratch copy of the data, and restores everything afterwards.

TRUST AND SAFETY BY DESIGN

- Every rule is tagged SOURCED, DEMO or BASELINE. DEMO rules are our prototype choices, labelled "Demo rule", and never attributed to NASA.

- All crew members, readings and events are fictional and simulated.

- Mood and wellbeing answers are private by default and shared only by the owner's choice. Emergency symptoms are never hidden.

- Vivonaut is an educational prototype, not a medical device. Viva never diagnoses and never replaces a crew medical officer, flight surgeons or approved mission procedures. It is not made, endorsed or reviewed by NASA.

NASA RESOURCES THAT MADE IT POSSIBLE

- NASA Human Research Program: the five hazards and the risk pages defined which health domains Vivonaut covers.

- NASA Technical Reports Server evidence reports and OCHMO technical briefs guided the indicators, the symptoms we watch and the wording of the explanations.

- NASA-STD-3001 (space permissible exposure limit) is the basis of the limit used for the simulated radiation dose.

- NASA studies on communication delays and blackouts (ASCEND) and on crew autonomy shaped the Delayed and Blackout modes and the handover idea.

- NASA Human Research Roadmap gap Medical-701 and the Spaceflight Standard Measures programme review support the project rationale.

Space agency partner material: ESA's Mars500 isolation study overview and ESA's exercise countermeasure (ARED) material. Every source, with the codes shown on the app's Sources page, is in docs/RESOURCES.md in our repository.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Vivonaut combines three roles that are usually separate: a companion that talks with the astronaut, a follow-up loop that checks whether a change persists, and a handover that works without Earth. It is honest by design: it labels what is sourced, what is a demo rule and what is simulated, and it explains every alert. It works offline from one file.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in one self-contained file. No libraries, no CDN, no server, no paid API, and no AI service while the app runs. Icons, the Viva robot, the logo, the charts and the body figure are original SVG drawn in code. Fonts are system fonts. Voice uses the browser's built-in speechSynthesis. We tested automatically with Playwright (headless Chrome) and Node.js.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

- Claude (Anthropic) assisted with planning, writing and testing the code (the file's header and the AI-use log say so) and with drafting text, under team direction. The concept, research direction, design decisions, testing and review are by Team Vivonaut.

- ChatGPT (OpenAI) generated the reference mockup image used as a visual guide. It carries a visible "Generated with ChatGPT" watermark wherever it is shown. The app does not copy it.

- Gemini (Google) was used occasionally for quick questions and idea checks. No application code, text or images were generated with it.

- The full phase-by-phase log is in docs/AI_USE_LOG.md. No NASA logo, flag or mission identifier is used.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

Reference ranges are general Earth-adult values and the DEMO rules are not clinically validated. The app has been tested automatically and checked independently, but real phones, other browsers and real voices have had little human testing. Next steps: evaluation with clinicians and crew-like users, clinical validation of the rules, wearable connectivity, and secure synchronisation with ground staff. A real point-of-care blood analysis device is a concept for the future. The same offline, explainable approach could also support remote communities on Earth where care is far away.

TRY IT IN THREE MINUTES

Open the live demo in any modern browser and press "Guided Demo" in the top bar. Then open Handover, press "Generate Health Handover" and "Ground view (simulation)". In Settings, choose the Drift scenario to see a Watch alert with "How Viva decided". It also works offline once opened.
